rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet and his close Companions called the surah Ta-Sin, after its opening letter-symbols.
rows.anchor: The Prophet and most of his close Companions used to refer to this surah as Ta-Sin

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Later Muslims called it An-Naml after a word in verse 18, whose link to Solomonic legends captivated readers and listeners.
rows.anchor: In later times, however, it came to be known as

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an uses legends as vehicles for allegories expressing universal ethical truths, as Asad also observes in his note on 21:82.
rows.anchor: the Qur'an often employs such legends as a vehicle for allegories expressing certain universal ethical truths

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because these legends were embedded in pre-Islamic Arab poetic memory as cultural realities, confirming or denying their mythical origins is irrelevant.
rows.anchor: they had become so firmly embedded in the poetic memories of the Arabs

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: What matters is each legend's layered spiritual truth, which the Qur'an presents explicitly, elliptically, or allegorically to reveal depths and conflicts in the human psyche.
rows.anchor: of the hidden depths and conflicts

rows.speaker: most authorities
rows.claim: Most authorities place An-Naml in the middle Meccan period, shortly after the preceding surah.
rows.anchor: In the consensus of most of the authorities, An-Naml belongs to the middle Mecca period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad inserts ‘God says’ at the start of verse 31, interpreting Solomon's command as God's speech through His prophet.
rows.anchor: My interpolation, at the beginning of this verse, of the words "God says"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: With no earlier contact between the kingdoms, Solomon had no reason to warn Sheba against exalting itself over him; the hoopoe instead says they exalted God by sun-worship and refusing to worship Him, so the prophet's call is justified. The wording echoes 44:19.
rows.anchor: In the absence of any previous contact, hostile or otherwise, there would have been no point whatever

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase means that the city's people were unaware at that time.
rows.anchor: Lit., "at a time of its people's unawareness"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses' phrase ‘his own people’ refers to the Hebrews.
rows.anchor: I.e., of the Hebrews

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad links ‘Satan's doing’ to his note on 15:17; verses 16–17 show that the Israelite, rather than the Egyptian, was in the wrong.
rows.anchor: Regarding the reference to "Satan's doing", see first half of note 16 on 15:17

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Moses instinctively helped his fellow Israelite from racial kinship without judging the case, then recognized he had killed an innocent person and acted from tribal prejudice.
rows.anchor: Moses had come to the assistance of the Israelite out of an instinctive sense of racial kinship

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet condemned proclaiming, fighting, or dying for tribal partisanship; Abu Da'ud reports this on Jubayr ibn Mut'im's authority.
rows.anchor: the Prophet on many occasions: cf. his famous saying, "He is not of us who proclaims the cause

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: The Prophet defined tribal partisanship as helping one's own people in an unjust cause; Abu Da'ud reports this on Wathilah ibn al-Asqa's authority.
rows.anchor: the Prophet answered, "It means helping thine own people in an unjust cause"

rows.speaker: Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil
rows.claim: Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil, as quoted by Baghawi, take this as indicating that the Israelite Moses helped was a denier of truth in the moral sense.
rows.anchor: According to Ibn 'Abbas and Muqatil (both of them quoted by Baghawi)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad offers an alternate rendering: God's praise is due in this present life as well as in the life to come.
rows.anchor: in this first [i.e., present life] as well as in the life to come

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Earth's many facilities for human life leave no excuse for forgetting God under adverse circumstances.
rows.anchor: the earth offers innumerable, multiform facilities to human life, there is no excuse for forgetting God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If essential worship becomes impossible, believers must leave the domain of evil and migrate to a place where they can live by their faith; this is the inner meaning of hijrah.
rows.anchor: the believer is obliged to "forsake the domain of evil"

rows.speaker: most authorities
rows.claim: Almost all authorities place As-Sajdah in the late Meccan period and say it followed surah 23 immediately.
rows.anchor: ALMOST all the authorities agree in that this

rows.speaker: some commentators
rows.claim: Some commentators assign verses 16–20 to Medina, a view Asad rejects as purely speculative and undeserving of serious consideration.
rows.anchor: The view advanced by some commentators that verses 16-20 were revealed at Medina is purely speculative

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah's title, As-Sajdah, comes from a key word in verse 15.
rows.anchor: The key-word which came to be accepted as the "title" of this surah is found in verse 15

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: By denying their meeting with God, the speakers also imply that they deny His existence, as discussed in notes 11–12 on 13:5.
rows.anchor: Sc., "and thus, by implication, they deny His existence"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad dates Saba to the second half of the Meccan period, probably shortly before surah 17.
rows.anchor: ALMOST certainly, this surah was revealed in the second half of the Mecca period

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its title refers to the people of Saba, cited in verses 15–20 as an example of the impermanence of human power, wealth, and glory.
rows.anchor: who are cited as an example of impermanence of all human power, wealth and glory

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The surah asks whether people notice how little of the heavens and earth is visible to them and how much remains hidden.
rows.anchor: how little of the sky and the earth lies open before them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It calls people to remain conscious of standing before God whether they are with others or alone.
rows.anchor: Be ever conscious of standing before God whether you are in the company of others or alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage rejects anyone who would mediate between God and any of His creatures.
rows.anchor: anybody who would "mediate" between Him and any of His creatures

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Its sequence and 17:56–57 show a particular concern with giving saints or angels divine or semi-divine status and claiming their intercession with God.
rows.anchor: this passage relates, in particular, to the attribution of divine or semi-divine qualities to saints and angels

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's question to the angels is allegorical, since He is omniscient and has no need to ask.
rows.anchor: This allegorical "question" - allegorical, because God is omniscient and has no need to "ask"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Many who reject God's messages delude themselves that they are worshipping spiritual forces, here called angels.
rows.anchor: many of "those who deny the truth" of God's messages delude themselves into believing

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels would never have accepted worship that is due to God alone.
rows.anchor: they (the angels) would never have accepted that worship which is due to God alone

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Here jinn primarily means what is concealed from human senses, including real or imagined unknown forces believed inherent in nature.
rows.anchor: the term jinn has its primary meaning of "that which is concealed from [man's] senses"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The angels' answer implies that alleged worship of them was a subconscious screen for fear of unseen natural forces and, ultimately, the Unknown.
rows.anchor: a subconscious screen for their fear of the invisible forces of nature and, ultimately, of the yet deeper fear of the Unknown

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who reject God's existence cannot see meaning or purpose in human life, and fear of the Unknown eventually engulfs them.
rows.anchor: all who refuse to believe in the existence of God and, hence, cannot see any meaning or purpose in human life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The literal wording is ‘who is following the reminder.’
rows.anchor: Lit., "who is following the reminder"

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Asad renders salam here as ‘peace and fulfilment,’ the closest English equivalent in context; he directs readers to his note on 5:16, where it is ‘salvation.’
rows.anchor: This composite expression is, I believe, the nearest approach in English

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For Asad's explanation of what the Qur'an means by ‘worship of Satan,’ see his note 33 on 19:44.
rows.anchor: For the meaning of what the Qur~a~n describes as "worship of Satan", see note 33 on 19: 44
